name: Cypriot Greek
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Arvaniti, Amalia. 1999. Cypriot Greek. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 29(2): 173-178 (Illustrations of the IPA). doi:10.1017/S002510030000654X
catalog_quote: Cypriot Greek has dynamic stress. There is only one stress per word, and it can fall on any of the word's last four syllables. Stress on the fourth syllable from the end of a word is rare and normally limited to certain verb forms. Because of this possibility, however, when words with antepenultimate stress are followed by an enclitic in Cypriot Greek, no extra stress is added (as happens in Standard Greek; see companion illustration); e.g. ... 'my bicycle'.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in the CUP PDF we hold of Arvaniti 1999 at printed p. 177 under 'Stress' (PDF page 5), exactly as cited. (2) Deciding source: a 1999 JIPA Illustration by the field's specialist on Greek/Cypriot prosody; primary, recent enough, and explicit on one-stress-per-word, free placement within the last four syllables, and absence of enclitic-induced extra stress. Glottolog has zero descriptive refs for cypr1249; web search surfaced Newton 1972 (full phonology monograph), Arvaniti 2010 (review chapter) and instrumental prosody papers (Themistocleous 2008 ExLing, 2016 Language and Speech; Arvaniti/Armosti on geminates) none of which re-describe stress placement in a way that would alter a lexical classification. tone.quote: In declaratives, the two nuclear pitch accents !H* and L+H* signal broad and narrow focus, respectively (Themistocleous, 2011). ... Postlexical prominence in polar questions associates with a low plateau: an L* pitch accent. ... The prosodic word consists of a content word and its clitics. The stressed syllable is specified in the lexicon (e.g., álla [ˈalːa] ‘other’ – allá [aˈlːa] ‘but’); unlike SMG, CG does not favour enclitic stress.

tone.quote: Το σύστημα τονισμού του ιδιώματος και της διαλέκτου γενικότερα είναι μορφολογικά καθορισμένο και ανήκει στα συστήματα λεξικού τονισμού, όμοια με την ΚΝΕ. Σε αυτά τα συστήματα η θέση του τόνου μέσα στη λέξη καθορίζεται από τη δυνατότητα ή μη ορισμένων μορφημάτων να φέρουν τόνο ή να προκαλούν μετακίνησή του εντός της λέξης. [...] Κ2. Ύπαρξη ιδιαίτερου επιτονισμού στον λόγο των ομιλητών [...]. Ο επιτονισμός αυτός χαρακτηρίζει το δυτικό άκρο του νησιού (Πάφος και Τυλληρία). Είναι ιδιαίτερα αισθητός σε φράσεις όπου η τελευταία τους λέξη τονίζεται στην παραλήγουσα, προσδίδοντας στο τονιζόμενο φωνήεν ιδιαίτερο τονικό ύψος και μεγαλύτερη διάρκεια.
tone.locator: p. 37, ch. 2 'Geniki perigrafi', section 2.1.2 'Tonismos kai epitonismos'; geographic note on the intonation isogloss pp. 43-45 (section 2.1.5, map 2-3)
tone.translation: The stress (accent) system of the local variety, and of the dialect more generally, is morphologically determined and belongs to the lexical-accent systems, like Standard Modern Greek. In these systems the position of the stress within the word is determined by the ability or not of certain morphemes to bear stress or to cause it to move within the word. [...] K2. Existence of a distinctive intonation in the speakers' speech [...]. This intonation characterises the western end of the island (Paphos and Tilliria). It is especially noticeable in phrases whose last word is stressed on the penult, giving the stressed vowel a distinctive pitch height and greater duration.
tone.summary: No statement on lexical tone; classifies NW-Paphos/Cypriot Greek as a lexical stress-accent system like SMG; pitch height appears only as a regional intonational feature on penult-stressed phrase-final words.

tone.quote: Specifically, the Cypriot Greek question tune consists of a low (L*) nuclear pitch accent that aligns at the most prominent syllable of the utterance, an H- phrase accent and a low (L%) boundary tone (Arvaniti et al, 2006; Baltazani, 2007; Grice et al, 2000; Themistocleous, 2011).
tone.summary: Intonational only: question tune L* H- L%; HRT L*+H-L%; calling tune L+H*!H%.

sources.citation: Themistocleous, Charalambos & Stelios Kyriacou. 2010. Focus prominence and tonal alignment in Athenian and Cypriot Greek. In: Proceedings of the 3rd ISCA Tutorial and Research Workshop on Experimental Linguistics (ExLing 2010), Athens (Linguistic Proceedings Series 3): 181-184. doi:10.36505/exling-2010/03/0046/000166

tone.quote: Focus is manifested in speech as a post-lexical prominence realized intonationally by the exploitation of nuclear pitch accents and phrase accents ... AG and CG productions show apparent similarities in the realization of focus prominence (see Figure 2). A rise and a fall are associated with the stressed syllable of the lexical constituent in focus. The local minimum of the F0 contour aligns at the onset of the stressed syllable, while the local maximum of the F0 contour aligns at the onset of the post-stressed syllable
tone.summary: No lexical tone; intonational pitch accents (rise-fall) dock on lexically stressed syllables; phrase accents/boundary tones.

sources.citation: Arvaniti, Amalia. 1998. Phrase accents revisited: comparative evidence from Standard and Cypriot Greek. In: Proceedings of the 5th International Conference on Spoken Language Processing (ICSLP 1998), Sydney, paper 0550. doi:10.21437/ICSLP.1998-161

tone.quote: From a phonological point of view, Cypriot Greek PQs have the same intonational structure as Standard Greek (and Hungarian) PQs: as can be seen in Figure 1, they exhibit a dip on the nuclear syllable and a rise-fall movement that occurs towards the end of the utterance. As in the other two languages, this contour can be autosegmentally described as L* H L%, i.e. as consisting of a L* pitch accent reflected in the F0 dip, and a sequence of a H phrase accent followed by a L% boundary tone, which together form the final rise-fall.
tone.locator: p. 1 of 4 (section 1, Introduction); alignment result restated p. 4 (section 4, Discussion and conclusion): 'Under canonical conditions, the Cypriot Greek H phrase accent associates with a specific TBU in a stable manner, on average 30ms into the penultimate or the final vowel of the utterance.'
tone.summary: Intonation only: CG polar questions = L* H L%; pitch accents dock on lexically stressed syllables; H phrase accent non-stress-seeking (penult/final vowel); nothing on lexical tone.
